content: 1. The primary screening test for cervical cancer prevention can involve the detection of HPV DNA. If the test result is positive, a triage process using dual-stain cytology (p16/Ki-67) is recommended. If the triage test is also positive, colposcopy should be performed to guide further management decisions. 2. Alternatively, HPV mRNA testing can be used as the primary screening test. A positive result should also be followed by triage with dual-stain cytology, and if necessary, colposcopy to determine the appropriate course of action. 3. These two algorithms (HPV DNA and HPV mRNA testing) have been integrated into a single flowchart for clinical use. Additionally, a separate algorithm is provided for follow-up testing 12 months after treatment. 4. In a screen-and-treat approach, treatment decisions are based solely on a positive primary screening test result. In contrast, the screen, triage, and treat approach requires a positive primary screening test followed by a positive triage test, with or without histological confirmation, to decide on treatment. 5. For women with a negative HPV DNA nucleic acid test (NAT), rescreening is recommended every 5 to 10 years. If HPV mRNA NAT is used, rescreening should occur every 5 years. 6. For women treated with ablation or large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) without histopathology results, or those treated based on histopathology confirming CIN 2/3 or AIS, follow-up testing is recommended at 12 months post-treatment. A negative result allows return to routine screening intervals, while a positive result necessitates further evaluation, biopsy, and management. 7. The WHO recommends using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test over visual inspection with acetic acid (VIA) or cytology for both the general population of women and women living with HIV. This is a strong recommendation based on moderate-certainty evidence. 8. In a screen-and-treat approach using HPV DNA detection, women who test positive for HPV DNA should be treated promptly. In a screen, triage, and treat approach, triage options such as partial genotyping, colposcopy, VIA, or cytology can be used after a positive HPV DNA test. The choice of triage method depends on feasibility, training, quality assurance, and available resources. 9. For women living with HIV, the WHO suggests starting regular cervical cancer screening at the age of 25 years. Screening should continue every 3 to 5 years, depending on the method used. After the age of 50, screening can be stopped if two consecutive negative results have been obtained within the recommended intervals. 10. Priority should be given to screening women aged 30–49 years in the general population. For women living with HIV, screening should begin earlier, at age 25. 11. The WHO suggests a regular screening interval of every 5 to 10 years for the general population of women when using HPV DNA detection as the primary screening test. For women living with HIV, the interval should be every 3 to 5 years. 12. Even in settings transitioning to a program with regular screening intervals, screening just twice in a lifetime can provide significant benefits for both the general population and women living with HIV. 13. Once a decision to treat is made, it is recommended to initiate treatment as soon as possible, ideally within six months, to minimize the risk of loss to follow-up. However, for pregnant women, treatment should be deferred until after pregnancy. 14. For women with histologically confirmed adenocarcinoma in situ (AIS), the WHO recommends treatment with large-loop excision of the transformation zone (LLETZ) or cold knife conization (CKC). Loop excision may be preferred for women of reproductive age or in settings with greater availability and expertise in LLETZ. 15. The WHO suggests that HPV mRNA detection using clinician-collected samples may be used as a primary screening test for cervical cancer prevention in the general population of women, with regular screening every 5 years. However, HPV DNA remains the preferred screening test. 16. No recommendation has been made for the use of HPV mRNA testing in women living with HIV due to insufficient evidence on its outcomes in this population. 17. As programs introduce HPV DNA testing, it should be used at the woman’s next routine screening date, regardless of the test used previously. In existing programs using cytology or VIA as the primary screening test, rescreening with the same test should continue until HPV DNA testing becomes operational.
